title: Same border, different truths
hook: Every map takes a side. Here are six places where it shows.
notes: Simplified. Kashmir shares: ≈ India 55%, Pakistan 30%, China 15% of the territory. Taiwan: recognised by 12 states incl. the Holy See (2024); smaller recognisers are islands too small for this map. Kosovo: recognition counts vary by source. Map makers such as Google show different borders depending on the country you view from.

scenes.title: Western Sahara, as the UN sees it
scenes.text: The UN lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory. Its status has been disputed since Spain withdrew in 1975.

scenes.title: Western Sahara, as Morocco sees it
scenes.text: Maps sold in Morocco show one country, no border. Morocco controls most of the territory. The United States recognised Moroccan sovereignty in 2020.

scenes.title: Kashmir
scenes.text: India, Pakistan and China each administer part of Kashmir, and the two largest each claim more. Indian maps show all of it as Indian; Pakistani maps differ.

scenes.title: Crimea
scenes.text: Russia annexed Crimea in 2014. In a 2014 UN General Assembly vote, 100 countries affirmed Ukraine's territorial integrity; most maps still show it as Ukraine.

scenes.title: Taiwan
scenes.text: Taiwan governs itself, while Beijing claims it. Only about a dozen states recognise Taiwan officially; those large enough to see on this map are highlighted.

scenes.title: Kosovo
scenes.text: Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008. Roughly half of UN members recognise it; Serbia, Russia, China and five EU states do not.
